options.counterfactual: Weak cototality does not always imply that the skip has cototal degree; there is a weakly cototal enumeration degree whose skip is not cototal.
options.approach: Audit the claimed weak-cototality implication directly from the definitions, carefully distinguishing a set of total degree from a representative whose complement is enumeration reducible to it. Identify the precise additional result needed before drawing any conclusion about the requested set.

options.counterfactual: Weak cototality does not always imply that the skip has cototal degree; there is a weakly cototal enumeration degree whose skip is not cototal.
options.approach: Investigate whether a counterexample can be chosen in Π₂⁰. Combine such an existence result with the facts that every Π₂⁰ degree is weakly cototal and every Σ₂⁰ degree is cototal to determine the exact complexity thresholds.

options.counterfactual: Weak cototality does not always imply that the skip has cototal degree; there is a weakly cototal enumeration degree whose skip is not cototal.
options.approach: Develop a direct construction of a weakly cototal set whose skip is not cototal, using requirements that diagonalize against all proposed enumeration reductions from the second skip to the first. Track the quantifier complexity of the construction to determine which arithmetical classes contain witnesses.

options.counterfactual: The characterization that an enumeration degree is cototal exactly when a representative is enumeration reducible to its skip is false.
options.approach: Recheck both directions of the proposed characterization using the universal diagonal set and the parameter theorem. Isolate any invalid passage involving complements of enumeration-equivalent sets.

options.counterfactual: The characterization that an enumeration degree is cototal exactly when a representative is enumeration reducible to its skip is false.
options.approach: Avoid the characterization and formulate noncototality directly: every representative of the skip degree must fail to be enumeration reducible to its complement. Examine whether a construction can meet these stronger-looking requirements explicitly.

options.counterfactual: The characterization that an enumeration degree is cototal exactly when a representative is enumeration reducible to its skip is false.
options.approach: Determine the correct relationship between cototality and the skip, allowing joins or a change of representative if necessary. Recompute the exclusions at the lowest arithmetical levels using that corrected relationship.

options.counterfactual: There are weakly cototal degrees with noncototal skips, but no Π₂⁰ set represents such a degree.
options.approach: Look for a special obstruction showing that every Π₂⁰ set has a cototal skip, without extending that obstruction to all weakly cototal degrees. Then investigate whether a Δ₃⁰ construction supplies the first witnesses.

options.counterfactual: There are weakly cototal degrees with noncototal skips, but no Π₂⁰ set represents such a degree.
options.approach: Analyze how the complexity of a weak-cototality witness changes when replacing a set by an enumeration-equivalent representative. Determine whether a higher-complexity counterexample can be lowered to Π₂⁰ or whether that lowering requires an unavailable inversion theorem.

options.counterfactual: There are weakly cototal degrees with noncototal skips, but no Π₂⁰ set represents such a degree.
options.approach: Separate the Σ and Π thresholds instead of assuming that one follows immediately from the other. Establish lower bounds for each hierarchy and seek a construction with an explicitly controlled membership formula.
